lens: DESIGN-RULE-FIT — BATTERIES-WITH-EJECT (REACHABILITY). I tried to refute that this design honors the REAL rule (raw wgpu + raw input + runtime-free primitives stay one property/reference away; nothing hidden behind an opaque abstraction; the interaction layer stays optional; nothing submitted/presented without consumer override). Owning/compositing the frame is sanctioned; only HIDING capability or CLOSING the eject is a violation. Verified every load-bearing repo claim against source: FrameLoop.cs (DriveFrame ordering, sealed-not-partial), Frame.cs (raw Pass/View/Encoder), FrameOutcome.cs (union exists), AppWindow.cs (public input events + plain ClipboardText + FrameGeom volatile pattern), WindowSurface.cs (Present is internal-to-loop), GpuContext.cs (raw handle eject), FrameLoopOptions.cs (BeginClearPass real).

topProblems.problem: OnOverlay's battery path presents the overlay's pixels with NO consumer-visible or overridable submit/present. DriveFrame (FrameLoop.cs:207-211) owns CommandEncoderFinish -> QueueSubmit -> present() as one opaque block. The design correctly places OnOverlay in the real seam between pass-end (line 205) and Finish (line 207), so the DRAW is reachable. But once the overlay encodes via OnOverlay, the loop submits AND presents those overlay pixels with zero consumer hook in between. For the BeginClearPass=true app that opts into the battery, the approvals modal gets composited and presented behind the consumer's back: the consumer who set loop.OnOverlay = overlay.Encode cannot see, gate, or veto that the overlay drew, and cannot intercept the present that ships it. This is exactly the lens's 'something submitted/presented with NO way for the consumer to see or override it' — the overlay is a frame-owning layer (sanctioned) but the present of ITS output is not reachable on the battery path. The Picture-B path escapes this (consumer owns the encoder and calls present themselves), but the design markets OnOverlay as the ergonomic default for the common app, and on that default the overlay's output reaches the screen with no eject.
topProblems.fix: Do not let the battery path present the overlay without a consumer seam. Two acceptable fixes: (a) Make OnOverlay return a bool or hand the consumer a 'pre-present' callback so the consumer can inspect/cancel before SurfacePresent runs — i.e. expose the present the way FrameLoop already exposes the clear pass and encoder. Or (b) Drop OnOverlay entirely and route the overlay ONLY through the existing BeginClearPass=false compositing path (open question 2's purist position), where the consumer already owns encode+submit+present and nothing is hidden. The design's own risk list flags this; resolve it toward (b) or toward (a) with an explicit present seam, because as written the common-app battery violates 'nothing presented behind your back.'

topProblems.problem: The IApprovalShell decision (policy verdict + the actual CapabilityGrant minted + what the overlay submitted as a ConsentRecord) is reachable to OVERRIDE (swap IApprovalPolicy, swap IApprovalUi) but the design gives no raw read seam for a consumer that KEEPS the battery yet wants to observe what was granted/denied without replacing it. The eject story is 'replace the whole policy or the whole UI.' That is wholesale, not one-property reachability. A consumer who likes Skyline's overlay and default policy but needs to log/audit/veto an individual grant the shell is about to mint has no documented hook short of reimplementing IApprovalPolicy or IApprovalUi. Reachability means the capability is one property away, not 'fork the battery.'
topProblems.fix: Add a non-replacing observation/veto seam on the shell: an event or callback (e.g. GrantMinted / BeforeGrant returning a bool) so a consumer keeping the default battery can see and override an individual decision, mirroring how ClearColor is settable without replacing the clear pass. Keep IApprovalPolicy/IApprovalUi as the wholesale ejects, but add the granular read/veto so 'see and override what a helper submits' holds at grant granularity, not only at policy granularity.

topProblems.problem: GPU-texture transfer has no honest home, and the design's own primitive REQUIRES a CPU round-trip — directly contradicting project memory ('textures must never round-trip to CPU'). ITransferRepresentation.OpenReadAsync returns Stream / ValueTask<Stream> (a byte stream). For AgentStaging/DragDropSession of a wgpu texture, that forces bytes, i.e. a GPU->CPU readback (TextureReadback exists exactly for pixel tests, not hot-path transfer). The design acknowledges this needs a Skyline.Interaction.Gpu bridge but defers it to an open question, so the canonical copy/paste-of-a-surface flow that motivates the whole 'who owns this transfer' model is NOT first-class for the one payload type Starling actually moves zero-copy. This is not a reachability violation per se, but it is a foundation-vs-facet contradiction: the transfer broker is sold as the home for the canonical flow, yet its representation contract cannot carry the canonical payload without violating the zero-copy constraint.
topProblems.fix: Either (a) define the GPU-handle representation seam NOW (a second representation interface that yields a wgpu Texture*/TextureView* handle, living in a Skyline.Interaction.Gpu bridge that depends on Skyline.Gpu, keeping Skyline.Interaction GPU-free) and make the broker prefer it; or (b) explicitly scope the broker to text/metadata transfers in v1 and state plainly that GPU-surface handoff is out of scope until the bridge exists — do not imply the canonical surface copy/paste is handled when only text is. Pick one before claiming the transfer model is first-class.

topProblems.problem: The code sketch declares 'public sealed partial class FrameLoop' but FrameLoop is sealed-NOT-partial today (FrameLoop.cs:19 is 'public sealed unsafe class FrameLoop'), and the OnOverlay field/invoke do not exist. So the 'only ONE sanctioned change to Skyline.Render' is real and does touch a core-three project. The design is honest that this is the one place the interaction tier reaches DOWN, and argues the hook 'names nothing from the interaction guide' (signature is TextureView*/CommandEncoder*). That defense is correct and the hook itself hides no wgpu. But the sketch is wrong as written (partial), and more importantly the justification leans on 'it's a pure wgpu seam' while the actual behavioral cost (the opaque present in problem 1) is what makes it more than a pure seam. The seam's SIGNATURE is clean; the seam's CONSEQUENCE (auto-submitted/presented overlay) is the violation.
topProblems.fix: If OnOverlay stays, fix the sketch (no partial; one field + one Invoke in DriveFrame) and pair it with the present seam from problem 1 so the hook is genuinely pure (hands view+encoder, and lets the consumer see the present). If the present seam is rejected, route through BeginClearPass=false and add NO new Skyline.Render member, which keeps the core-three change at zero — the strictly safer reachability posture.

topProblems.problem: Concurrent pending approvals are resolved by drawing/hit-testing only Pending[^1] (top of stack), which can starve or reorder a lower request and leave its TaskCompletionSource parked. Combined with the park-the-asker suspend in ShellActor, a request that never gets surfaced (because a newer one keeps landing on top) hangs the requesting actor until its 30s deadline. This is a correctness/liveness bug in the consent state machine, not a rule-fit violation, but it undermines the 'authority is enforced deterministically at one chokepoint' selling point.
topProblems.fix: Specify deterministic ordering and guarantee every parked request resolves: FIFO surfacing (not LIFO top-of-stack), mandatory ExpiresAt timeout that fires for EVERY pending request (not just the visible one), and prune-on-resolve so the next request is surfaced immediately. Add a windowed-harness test that stacks two requests on different threads and asserts both TaskCompletionSources complete.

topProblems.problem: Akka as the home of the only IInteractionShell would make a heavy actor framework MANDATORY to use the shell at all, inverting batteries-with-eject (the battery becomes too big to be the default and there is no lighter battery underneath). The foundation lists Skyline.Interaction.Akka as 'the runtime that turns the primitives into a live system' with no non-Akka shell; only the facets later propose a lightweight InProcessShell. If a consumer must pull Akka.NET to get ANY working shell, the ten-line ethos and the 'optional, additive' claim weaken — the primitives are reachable runtime-free, but a RUNNING shell is not.
topProblems.fix: Make the lightweight non-Akka InProcessShell (a plain async IInteractionShell over the pure primitives, lock-guarded FocusGraph + Channel<InteractionIntent>) the DEFAULT battery shipped in Skyline.Interaction, with Akka as the explicit opt-in scale-up for remote/collaboration. Put the shared policy/arbitration in pure functions in Skyline.Interaction (already proposed) so neither shell re-implements rules. This keeps 'a running shell' one reference away without Akka.

whatToKeep: The hard split that keeps the core three uncorrupted is correct and verified: Skyline.Gpu gains no Actor/Focus/Target/Command/Transfer/Capability/Consent (stays a 1:1 wgpu mirror, raw Silk.NET handles in/out per GpuContext.cs), Skyline keeps emitting plain PointerEvent/KeyEvent/TextEvent and a plain ClipboardText string (verified in InputEvents.cs + AppWindow.cs:160-164), and the interaction vocabulary lives entirely one tier up. This is the load-bearing rule-fit win and it holds.

Subscribe-not-replace for raw input is genuinely eject-safe: AppWindow.PointerInput/KeyInput/TextInput are public events (AppWindow.cs:143-145), the interaction source subscribes without intercepting, so a consumer ignoring the whole tier reads raw structs exactly as today. ClipboardText stays a plain getter/setter the broker wraps rather than absorbs. Both are real one-property ejects.

Frame's raw Pass/View/Encoder stay reachable mid-frame (Frame.cs verified) and the BeginClearPass=false compositing path is real (FrameLoopOptions.cs:24) — the overlay riding the SAME CurrentView via a LoadOp.Load pass, not wrapping it, is the correct compositing posture and matches how FrameLoop already lets the consumer drop to raw wgpu.

Mapping each guide Actor 1:1 to an addressable Akka actor so 'every interaction says WHO' is structural (the sender's path is the identity, not a spoofable field) is a strong design idea, especially the single-writer FocusActor making 'a remote pointer cannot steal local focus' a structural guarantee rather than a convention. The identity-spoofing risk (reconcile msg.ActorId against Sender path) is correctly flagged.

The threading discipline reuses proven repo patterns honestly: immutable snapshot swapped through one volatile field (mirroring AppWindow's FrameGeom at AppWindow.cs:27-28), RequestRedraw as the any-thread wake (FrameLoop.cs:162), never calling wgpu or GLFW off their owning threads, and park-the-asker (not Ask().Result) to avoid PinnedDispatcher self-deadlock. Allocation-free idle path matches FramePacer's discipline.

Correctly treating ARCHITECTURE.md line 146 ('a library that owns the frame... never inside them') as the stale stance to REWRITE rather than design around, and stating the live rule as reachability with owning/compositing the frame sanctioned — this matches the updated owner-confirmed rule and prevents future contributors re-deriving the abstinence stance.
contradictions: Foundation says the transfer broker is the home for the canonical copy/paste flow ('a sequence of typed messages: eyes set Attention, voice says copy, shell resolves target, surface offers transfer, broker stores with policy, paste is brokered'), but the facet's ITransferRepresentation.OpenReadAsync returns a byte Stream, which forces a GPU->CPU round-trip for the one payload Starling moves zero-copy. The canonical flow's headline payload (a surface/texture) is unsupported by the very contract sold as its home, and project memory explicitly forbids the round-trip.

Foundation's ejectStory says 'Nothing the shell does is hidden — a consumer can see and override the grant prompts, the focus policy, and the present, just like FrameLoop already exposes its present.' But FrameLoop does NOT expose the present as an override seam — Present is called inside DriveFrame (FrameLoop.cs:211) with no consumer hook, and the new OnOverlay path adds overlay pixels to that same un-overridable present. The claim 'a consumer can override the present' is false today and the design does not add the seam that would make it true on the battery path.

Foundation lists Skyline.Interaction.Akka as THE runtime that implements the shell, implying Akka is required for a working shell, while the facets and overallGaps argue Akka must be opt-in with a lightweight non-Akka default shell. The foundation and facets disagree on whether a running shell is reachable without Akka — unresolved, and it determines whether 'the interaction layer is optional and additive' fully holds.

whatStaysOut says 'Skyline.Render must NOT gain interaction concepts... the only sanctioned change is the optional, null-by-default OnOverlay hook, which is a pure wgpu seam,' but the same design relies on OnOverlay to auto-composite-and-present the approvals overlay. A seam whose entire purpose is to ship a specific layer's pixels through the loop's hidden present is not purely a 'pure wgpu seam' in consequence even if its signature names nothing from the guide — the signature is clean, the behavioral coupling is not.

The code sketch declares 'public sealed partial class FrameLoop' but the repo has 'public sealed unsafe class FrameLoop' (FrameLoop.cs:19), non-partial. Minor, but the sketch as written would not compile against the actual declaration without also editing the existing class — the 'one additive change' is slightly more invasive than presented.

Foundation says the actor runtime is iOS-portable and drives 'from CADisplayLink with no FrameLoop' — but on iOS CADisplayLink.OnFrame runs ON the main run loop and does ALL wgpu work there (verified in BrowserViewController.OnFrame + PageRenderer.RenderFrame). The Akka facet's iOS story says input marshals 'to the UIKit main thread becomes DispatchQueue.main instead of AppHost.Invoke' and 'the shell runs there or on Akka's dispatcher'. If the shell runs on an Akka dispatcher, then a SurfaceActor deciding to draw must hand state to the main run loop where OnFrame reads it — the desktop 'render thread reads a volatile snapshot' pattern still works, BUT the facet never states that on iOS the 'render thread' IS the main thread, so a SurfaceActor that does AppWindow-style RequestRedraw has nothing to call (no FrameLoop, no AppWindow). The marshalling story is asserted to be identical but the iOS thread topology is fundamentally different (2 threads desktop: main+render; effectively 1 thread iOS: main does input AND render).

Approvals facet threadingNotes claims the human's answer 'arrives on the MAIN thread' and resolves the TCS, and that this 'mirrors AppWindow's main->render contract'. But AppWindowInteractionSource subscribes to AppWindow.PointerInput which fires during PollEvents on main — correct. However the same facet's OnPointerDown reads `_snapshot` (volatile, fine) AND calls Resolve which does RebuildSnapshot() — meaning the MAIN thread writes the snapshot that the RENDER thread reads every frame. That is the correct direction (main writes, render reads, mirroring FrameGeom). But RebuildSnapshot is ALSO called from RequestAsync on an arbitrary Akka thread. So the snapshot has TWO writers (main thread on resolve, Akka thread on request) and one reader (render). FrameGeom has exactly ONE writer (main). The facet calls this 'identical to FrameGeom' — it is not; two concurrent writers racing a non-atomic multi-step RebuildSnapshot (gather pending + live grants) can interleave and produce a lost update or a snapshot missing a just-added request.

The Akka facet puts ShellActor on a PinnedDispatcher and says delegation/authority decisions and the grant table live there, while the approvals facet has the overlay resolve a TaskCompletionSource that the ShellActor's ApprovalGate awaited with `await _ui.RequestAsync(...).ConfigureAwait(false)`. ConfigureAwait(false) plus RunContinuationsAsynchronously means the continuation resumes on a thread-pool thread, NOT the pinned shell thread — so the post-await code that mutates _grants and _pending now runs OFF the pinned dispatcher, racing any concurrent message the ShellActor is processing on its pinned thread. The two facets contradict: the Akka facet's design (park-the-asker, ApprovalAnswered as a message) keeps mutation on the dispatcher; the approvals facet's ApprovalGate.AuthorizeAsync (await then mutate) does NOT. Both are presented as the implementation.

ejectStory and approvals facet both assert wgpu is only ever touched on the render thread via OnOverlay/Encode. But the Akka facet's BrokerActor 'on desktop also writes AppWindow.ClipboardText via AppHost.Invoke' on OfferAsync. ClipboardText is GLFW (GetClipboardString/SetClipboardString on the GLFW handle) and MUST be main-thread — the facet correctly routes it through AppHost.Invoke. Good. But the approvals/foundation never reconcile that OfferAsync returning a Task that an actor awaits now depends on the main-thread pump draining the Invoke queue (Thread.Sleep(2) cadence) — if OfferAsync is awaited synchronously-ish in a hot path it adds up-to-2ms latency per clipboard write, and if the main loop is blocked (a long Invoke action, or the app not in AppHost.Run yet) the await never completes. Not a deadlock in the common case but a liveness coupling the design claims does not exist.
whatToKeep: The core split is sound and matches the repo's proven contract: input + shell-decision logic on the main/dispatcher threads, wgpu strictly on the render thread, and the cross-thread handoff done by (a) an immutable snapshot swapped through a single volatile reference and (b) the any-thread-safe RequestRedraw. This is a faithful copy of AppWindow's FrameGeom + AutoResetEvent pattern (verified in AppWindow.cs lines 27-31, 162-166) and is the right backbone.

Never blocking a dispatcher on a render result. The Akka facet explicitly forbids Ask().Result/.Wait() into the render thread and makes drawing fire-and-forget (flip snapshot, RequestRedraw, return). This correctly avoids the most obvious deadlock class. The PinnedDispatcher self-deadlock hazard is called out by name in the facet's risks, as is the PipeTo-only rule.

Modeling the approvals suspend as a parked asker (Akka facet: _pending dictionary keyed by ApprovalId, completed by an ApprovalAnswered MESSAGE) rather than a blocking await is the correct actor-model design — the dispatcher thread returns immediately and the mailbox stays live. This is the right answer and should be the canonical one (it conflicts with the approvals facet's await-based ApprovalGate, which is the wrong one).

FocusActor as the single writer of FocusGraph is a genuinely strong threading decision: it serializes all slot mutations through one mailbox, so a remote pointer arriving on a network thread and a local pointer arriving on the main thread cannot race the focus state. This converts a data-race-prone shared structure into a message-ordered one, which is exactly what the actor model is good for.

TaskCompletionSource(RunContinuationsAsynchronously) is correctly chosen to prevent the resolving thread (main thread, inside PollEvents) from being hijacked by the awaiting actor's continuation — without it, resolving on the main thread could run arbitrary continuation code inside the GLFW pump.

Keeping the primitives (Skyline.Interaction) free of any thread-affine type (no GLFW, no wgpu, no IActorRef) is what makes the headless MSTest coverage of the focus/authority/consent logic possible, and keeps the thread-correctness surface confined to the .Akka and .Ui assemblies.

topProblems.problem: iOS marshalling story does not hold as written. On iOS there is NO render thread: CADisplayLink's OnFrame runs on the main run loop and performs ALL wgpu work (verified: BrowserViewController.OnFrame calls PageRenderer.RenderFrame which does TryAcquireFrame/encode/QueueSubmit/Present, all on NSRunLoop.Main). The design repeatedly asserts the desktop 'render thread reads an immutable snapshot, input/shell run elsewhere' pattern is 'byte-for-byte identical' on iOS. It is not: input (OnPan) and render (OnFrame) are the SAME thread on iOS, while the shell, if run on an Akka dispatcher, is a DIFFERENT thread. So an Akka SurfaceActor or ApprovalsOverlay on a dispatcher that flips a volatile snapshot must have that snapshot read by OnFrame on the main thread — which works for a value/reference read, BUT any UIKit call (UIAlertController for the approvals UI, UIPasteboard for the broker) MUST be marshalled to the main thread, and the design's UIKitApprovalUi.RequestAsync hand-waves this as 'marshal to the UIKit main thread' without saying the actor that called it is on a dispatcher and the TCS will resolve from a UIAlertController action on main while the awaiting actor resumes on a dispatcher. The deeper problem: if the consumer chooses the InProcessShell (the recommended lightweight default) and runs it inline on the main thread for simplicity, then RequestPasteAsync/InvokeAsync that await an approval will DEADLOCK — the main thread is blocked in the await, so OnFrame never runs, the UIAlertController action never fires (UIKit needs the run loop), and the TCS is never resolved.
topProblems.fix: State the iOS thread topology explicitly and design for it: on iOS the 'render thread' IS the main run loop, so (1) the shell/broker MUST run on an Akka dispatcher (never inline on main) OR all awaits must be genuinely async and yield back to the run loop; (2) every UIKit touch (UIAlertController, UIPasteboard, address bar) marshals via DispatchQueue.MainQueue.DispatchAsync and resolves the TCS from there; (3) the InProcessShell must be documented as requiring a real async context on iOS and must never be awaited synchronously on the main thread. Add an iOS-specific integration test or at minimum a sample (Interaction.Ios) that exercises an approval round-trip on the run loop to prove no deadlock.

topProblems.problem: Two concurrent writers race the ApprovalSnapshot rebuild. The approvals facet calls RebuildSnapshot() from (a) RequestAsync on an arbitrary Akka dispatcher thread and (b) Resolve, which is invoked from OnPointerDown on the MAIN thread. RebuildSnapshot is a multi-step gather (pending requests + live grants) then an atomic swap. The design claims this is 'identical to how AppWindow rebuilds FrameGeom' — but FrameGeom has exactly ONE writer (the main thread, on resize). Here two threads can enter RebuildSnapshot concurrently: a new request arriving (Akka thread) while the human resolves the previous one (main thread). Without a lock around the gather+swap, the two rebuilds interleave and the last writer wins, silently dropping the other's change — e.g. a just-added pending request vanishes (its TCS now hangs forever because the overlay will never draw it), or a resolved request reappears. The volatile field makes the SWAP atomic but does nothing for the read-modify-write of the gather.
topProblems.fix: Serialize all snapshot mutation through a single owner. The cleanest fix that matches the Akka facet: make the ApprovalGate/ShellActor the sole writer — RequestAsync and Resolve both send MESSAGES (ApprovalRequested / ApprovalAnswered) to the gate actor, which rebuilds the snapshot on its own single thread and publishes the immutable result to the volatile field the render thread reads. Then there is exactly one writer again and the FrameGeom analogy actually holds. If a non-Akka InProcessShell is used, guard RebuildSnapshot with a lock (the gather is off the per-frame hot path, so a lock there is fine; the render-thread read stays lock-free).

topProblems.problem: ApprovalGate.AuthorizeAsync (approvals facet) mutates shell state after an await with ConfigureAwait(false), moving the mutation OFF the PinnedDispatcher and racing the ShellActor. The sketch does `var decision = await _ui.RequestAsync(req, ct).ConfigureAwait(false); return MakeGrant(...)` and the MakeGrant path in the Akka facet writes _grants/_pending. ConfigureAwait(false) plus the TCS's RunContinuationsAsynchronously guarantees the continuation runs on a thread-pool thread, not the actor's pinned thread. So _grants and _pending — described as hot mutable state owned by the pinned ShellActor — get mutated concurrently with whatever message the ShellActor is processing on its dispatcher. This is a classic 'await inside an actor handler touches actor state after the await' bug, which Akka explicitly warns against. The two facets even disagree: the Akka facet's park-the-asker design is correct; the approvals facet's await-then-mutate ApprovalGate is the bug.
topProblems.fix: Forbid awaiting external work inside an actor and then touching actor state. Adopt the Akka facet's park-the-asker pattern as the single canonical design: ShellActor stashes (Sender, request) in _pending, Tells the gate, returns; the gate/UI later Tells ApprovalAnswered, and ShellActor handles it ON its dispatcher, mutating _grants there and PipeTo-ing the result to the original asker. Delete the await-based ApprovalGate.AuthorizeAsync, or relocate it to a stateless helper that captures nothing and only returns a value the actor applies in a follow-up message handler.

topProblems.problem: Identity is carried as a spoofable ActorId field while the only trustworthy identity (the Akka Sender path) is not enforced at every authority boundary. The Akka facet acknowledges 'msg.ActorId is attacker-controllable; only Sender is trustworthy' and says ShellActor reconciles them — but the FocusActor sketch keys its local-vs-remote decision purely on `IsRemote(m.ActorId) => actorId.StartsWith("remote:")`, a string on the message, NOT on Sender. So a RemoteHumanActor (or a compromised source) can send UpdatePointer with ActorId='local-human' and the FocusActor will write the LOCAL Pointer slot — defeating the entire 'remote pointer cannot steal local focus' guarantee, which the design sells as a STRUCTURAL property. This is a threading/concurrency-adjacent correctness hole: the single-writer FocusActor is only as safe as the identity it trusts, and it trusts the wrong field.
topProblems.fix: Make the FocusActor (and every authority check) derive locality from Sender.Path (the actor address, which Akka authenticates within a node and via Akka.Remote across nodes), never from a message field. Either look up the source actor's known kind/locality from a registry keyed by Sender, or have each InputSourceActor be the only sender of its own slot updates so the FocusActor can validate Context.Sender == the expected local source ref before writing the local Pointer/Text slots.

topProblems.problem: Parked-approval and TCS leaks hang the requesting actor indefinitely if a wakeup is lost. Both facets rely on ExpiresAt/ReceiveTimeout to deny stale requests, but the wakeup paths have gaps: (a) on ShellActor restart (its SupervisorStrategy restarts faulting AI actors, and the shell itself could restart), the _pending dictionary is cleared by the restart, stranding every awaiting caller's Task with no completion — the design's own risk list notes this but offers no concrete mechanism; (b) the CancellationToken.Register(() => Resolve(..., Deny)) in the overlay's RequestAsync races with a normal Resolve — if both fire, TryRemove handles the double-resolve, but if the ct fires AFTER TryRemove already removed the waiter on a normal answer, the Deny is silently dropped (benign) — however if RebuildSnapshot raced (see blocker above) the waiter may never have been registered visibly; (c) the auto-expire is described as happening in the overlay/snapshot prune on the RENDER thread, but the render thread must NOT resolve TCSs or touch shell state — resolving on the render thread violates the design's own rule that the render thread only reads the snapshot.
topProblems.fix: Centralize all approval completion (answer, timeout, cancel, shell-restart) in ONE owner — the ApprovalGate actor — using Akka's scheduler for the timeout (Context.System.Scheduler.ScheduleTellOnce(deadline, Self, ApprovalTimedOut)) so timeouts are dispatcher messages, never render-thread work. On PreRestart/PostStop, the gate must drain _pending and complete every parked Task with a denied result so no caller hangs. The render thread must never call Resolve; it only reads the snapshot and may flag 'expired' visually, with actual resolution done by the gate.

topProblems.problem: Liveness coupling between actor awaits and the main-thread Invoke pump is undocumented and can stall. BrokerActor.OfferAsync 'also writes AppWindow.ClipboardText via AppHost.Invoke' (GLFW clipboard is main-thread-only, correctly routed). But AppHost drains its Invoke queue only inside Run's loop at a Thread.Sleep(2) cadence, and ONLY while Run is executing. So any actor awaiting the completion of a main-thread-marshalled operation is coupled to: (1) up-to-2ms latency per hop, and (2) the main loop actually running. If the clipboard write is fire-and-forget (Invoke returns void), there is no completion to await and it is fine; but if any design path awaits a main-thread result (e.g. reading ClipboardText for RequestPasteAsync fallback — a GETTER that must run on main), the actor blocks on a TCS resolved only by the main pump, and if the app is mid-teardown or the pump is blocked by a long prior Invoke action, the await never completes.
topProblems.fix: Make every main-thread-marshalled GLFW operation explicitly fire-and-forget where possible (clipboard SET), and for operations that must return a value (clipboard GET for paste fallback), wrap them as Invoke(() => { var s = window.ClipboardText; tcs.TrySetResult(s); }) with a timeout/cancellation so a stalled pump denies the paste rather than hanging. Document that no actor await may depend on the main pump without a timeout, and that the broker's clipboard mirror is best-effort.

topProblems.problem: FrameLoop.OnOverlay is invoked from DriveFrame on the render thread and is handed the live encoder/view, but the delegate target (ApprovalsOverlay.Encode) reads _snapshot/_pending which other threads write — the ordering guarantee that the overlay sees a request BEFORE the redraw it triggered is not actually established. RequestAsync does RebuildSnapshot() THEN _requestRedraw(). RequestRedraw does Volatile.Write(_dirty,1) then AppWindow.RequestRedraw (AutoResetEvent.Set). The render thread consumes _dirty via Interlocked.Exchange in the IsDirty gate, then later reads _snapshot in Encode. Because the snapshot write (volatile store) happens-before the redraw signal, and the render thread's dirty-read happens-before its snapshot-read, the overlay WILL see the new snapshot — this specific ordering is actually correct. BUT the reverse path (Resolve clears the modal then RequestRedraw) has the same shape and is also correct, so the real residual risk is only the multi-writer rebuild (blocker above), not the publish ordering. Flagging because the design asserts correctness without naming the happens-before chain that makes it true, so a future refactor that reorders RebuildSnapshot after RequestRedraw would silently break it.
topProblems.fix: Document the required ordering as a load-bearing invariant: snapshot store MUST precede the redraw signal (publish-before-notify), mirroring how AppWindow writes _pendingResize before RequestRedraw. Add a comment at both RequestAsync and Resolve, and a test that asserts a request issued just before a frame is visible to that frame's Encode.

topProblems.problem: Per-frame allocation discipline is asserted but the IAsyncEnumerable intent stream (WatchIntentsAsync) and the snapshot's IReadOnlyList allocations can leak onto hot paths. The approvals facet keeps the per-frame Encode path allocation-free (one volatile read + branch), which is correct. But the Akka facet's WatchIntentsAsync uses a bounded Channel with a per-subscriber relay actor, and InteractionIntent is a record (heap) produced for every accepted intent — at pointer-move rates (the highest-frequency source) this allocates one record per move, plus channel bookkeeping, on the dispatcher. The design notes 'drop-oldest for liveness' but not that producing an intent record per raw pointer move (which AppWindow emits on every MouseMove) will pressure the GC against the repo's per-frame allocation rule. This is a dispatcher-thread allocation concern, not a render-thread one, so it does not violate the FramePacer hot path — but it does undercut the 'allocation-conscious' norm under high-frequency input.
topProblems.fix: Coalesce high-frequency sources before they become intents: the MouseSourceActor should debounce/coalesce raw Move events into at most one Aim intent per frame tick (or per redraw), rather than one intent per OS move callback. Keep the raw PointerEvent path (which an app can still read directly) untouched; only throttle the intent translation. Consider a struct-based intent for the Aim/Move verb to avoid per-move heap allocation.

lens: SCOPE / OVER-ENGINEERING — measuring the proposed integration against a 2474-line library whose entire pitch is "ten lines to a GPU frame," and asking what the MINIMUM viable first-class integration is.

topProblems.problem: MASSIVE scope inversion. The entire Skyline library is 2474 lines across 3 projects (Skyline.Render, the most complex piece consumers ride, is 326 lines of real code). The design proposes 4 NEW projects plus 4 new test projects, a full Akka.NET actor runtime, ~600 lines of vocabulary primitives, a composited GPU approvals overlay with its own pipeline/glyph atlas, and a consent state machine — to satisfy ONE concrete user ask (Skyline owns the approvals UI for three scenarios). The new tier would dwarf the library it sits on. A 'getting-started-friendly' library does not bolt on an interaction framework an order of magnitude larger than itself as a first-class citizen. The design even concedes the guide is 'intentionally NOT a full UI framework' and then specs a full UI framework.
topProblems.fix: Ship v1 as ONLY what the user explicitly asked for: the approvals UI, behind one interface, with the smallest decision model that drives it. That is a single small project (Skyline.Interaction with IApprovalUi + IApprovalPolicy + ApprovalRequest/Decision/CapabilityGrant/ConsentRecord + DefaultApprovalPolicy, ~150 lines pure) plus the desktop overlay drawing. Defer Actor topology, FocusGraph, Target hierarchy, Command/CommandId, the full Transfer broker, Intents, and InputSnapshot to a v2 that ships ONLY if a real consumer (Starling) demands the primitive surface. The full guide is a design north star, not a v1 deliverable.

topProblems.problem: Akka.NET is treated as the runtime spine but is a mandatory-feeling heavy dependency the library should not have, and it is unjustified at v1's one-window scale. The design's OWN open questions and risks admit this three times. Akka earns its keep only at REMOTE/collaboration/multi-mailbox scale (Akka.Remote transport, supervised AI actors with addresses) — none of which v1 needs and none of which a single local window with a local human exercises. For 'an AI wants to type into a text field,' an actor tree with PinnedDispatchers, EventStream fan-out, IntentRelayActors, and supervision strategies is pure ceremony. The whole 'every interaction says WHO' guarantee is delivered by an ActorId field plus a trust check, not by a mailbox per participant. The design even notes msg.ActorId is spoofable and Sender must be reconciled — which means the actor address ISN'T free identity, it needs the same explicit check a plain shell would do.
topProblems.fix: Akka must NOT be a dependency of anything in v1, and ideally never a dependency the common consumer pulls. Make the default IInteractionShell a plain in-process implementation (lock-guarded state + a Channel for the intent stream) living in Skyline.Interaction with zero extra deps. Keep Skyline.Interaction.Akka as a SEPARATE opt-in package that exists only if/when remote collaboration is real. The approvals flow (RequestAsync awaiting a TaskCompletionSource) needs no actors at all — the design's own ApprovalGate sketch depends only on IApprovalUi/IApprovalPolicy. Akka should be demoted from 'the runtime' to 'a scale-up transport nobody needs yet.'

topProblems.problem: The primitive surface is far bigger than any known consumer needs. Starling — the ONLY concrete consumer — rides FrameLoop in Picture B and bypasses AppWindow entirely on iOS. Nothing in the Starling framing asks for FocusGraph's six slots, the Target hierarchy (Ray3D/Volume3D/Semantic), the CommandId namespace, Intents with 11 verbs, InputSnapshot, or the seven-scope Transfer broker. These are speculative generality lifted wholesale from an aspirational guide (gaze, voice, multi-actor collaboration) that has zero implementation behind it in this repo — no eye tracker, no speech engine, no remote transport, no AI actor. Building the vocabulary for inputs that do not exist yet is textbook over-engineering: every type is a maintenance and coverage burden (100% line coverage is GATED) for a capability with no caller.
topProblems.fix: Build only the primitives the approvals UI actually consumes: Actor (Id/Kind/Locality/DelegatedBy), InteractionCapability flags, CapabilityGrant, ConsentRecord, and a TargetRef-lite for the prompt to name what is being requested. Leave FocusGraph, the Target class hierarchy, CommandId, Intents, InputSnapshot, and the Transfer broker as documented-but-unbuilt until a consumer needs them. Add each primitive when its first real caller arrives, not before. This keeps the 100% coverage gate cheap and honest.

topProblems.problem: The composited GPU approvals overlay (own pipeline, glyph atlas, vertex caching, LoadOp.Load pass, ApprovalSnapshot volatile swap) is heavyweight first-class code for a battery that the design ITSELF admits is OPTIONAL and non-existent on iOS — where the proven, shipping pattern is native UIKit chrome over the wgpu page (verified: BrowserViewController already does exactly this with a real UITextField address bar). So the 'Skyline handles the approvals UI' promise is only true on desktop, and on desktop it requires Skyline to grow a mini-immediate-mode-GUI (text rendering, hit-testing, button layout) — capability this library has deliberately never had. That is a large new surface to own and test.
topProblems.fix: Make IApprovalUi the FIRST-class deliverable and the composited overlay a thin reference battery, not the centerpiece. On desktop, the minimum viable overlay can reuse the sample's existing pixel-font/HUD approach (HelloWindow already draws a text panel and verifies it via readback) rather than a new glyph-atlas pipeline — keep it deliberately ugly and small. Frame the honest scope: 'Skyline ships the approvals DECISION model and an IApprovalUi seam; desktop gets a built-in overlay battery, iOS plugs a native UIKitApprovalUi.' Do not oversell a composited GUI toolkit as a Skyline first-class citizen.

topProblems.problem: The FrameLoop.OnOverlay hook is a net-new public seam added to a core-three project that the design's own 'whatStaysOut' says must gain NO interaction concepts — and it is unnecessary. Verified: DriveFrame already exposes the entire composite path. BeginClearPass=false hands the consumer the raw encoder/view, and the overlay's Encode(view, encoder) is the SAME code with or without the hook. The hook exists only to spare BeginClearPass=true apps from compositing themselves, which is a convenience, not a requirement. Adding permanent public API to the most load-bearing file in the library for a convenience is scope creep into the core.
topProblems.fix: Do NOT add OnOverlay to FrameLoop in v1. Route the overlay through the existing BeginClearPass=false path (the purist position the design lists as open question 2). If real ergonomic pain shows up later for the common clear-pass app, add the hook then, as a deliberate core change with a caller. Keep the core three frozen until the interaction tier has proven itself outside the core.

whatToKeep: The dependency-direction discipline is correct and should survive any descoping: a pure, zero-dependency primitives tier (no Skyline/Gpu/Render/Silk/Akka) is the right shape and is what makes the model usable headless, on iOS, and in MSTest. Keep this rule even for the tiny v1.

IApprovalUi as the eject seam is the single best idea in the design. One interface, two batteries (composited desktop overlay, native UIKitApprovalUi), identical decision logic behind both — this is exactly batteries-with-eject and exactly how iOS stays clean. It should be the v1 centerpiece.

The three named scenarios collapsing into ONE parameterized prompt driven by CapabilityGrant flags (request-control / keyboard / type = Administer|LowLevelInput / Edit) is genuinely elegant and is the minimum that satisfies the user's explicit ask. Keep it.

The default policy table keyed on (ActorKind, ActorLocality) with overridable DefaultApprovalPolicy, and the structural rule that remote/AI never get Edit/LowLevelInput, is the right small authority model — and it does not need actors to be true.

The threading analysis (request on arbitrary thread -> TaskCompletionSource -> resolve on main thread; render thread reads one volatile immutable snapshot, mirroring AppWindow's FrameGeom; zero per-frame allocation when idle) is sound and correctly mirrors proven repo patterns. This is the part that respects Skyline's load-bearing contract and should be preserved verbatim.

The ARCHITECTURE.md line-146 amendment (a Skyline-family layer MAY own/composite the frame; the live rule is reachability, not abstinence) is correct and confirmed by the repo owner — worth doing regardless of how much of the rest ships, since FrameLoop already contradicts the stale line.

Keeping the core three (Skyline.Gpu raw wgpu mirror, Skyline plain input structs + ClipboardText, Skyline.Render) free of all interaction vocabulary is the right boundary and the design holds it (modulo the OnOverlay wrinkle).
contradictions: The design repeatedly names Akka.Interaction.Akka 'the runtime that turns the primitives into a live system' and gives it the ShellActor that implements IInteractionShell — i.e. the DEFAULT shell — yet its own risks and overallGaps say Akka is too heavy to be the default and a non-Akka in-process shell should exist. The foundation and the facets disagree on whether Akka is mandatory. As written, a consumer who wants ANY shell pulls Akka; the mitigation (lightweight InProcessShell) is mentioned only as a risk-mitigation afterthought, not built into the architecture.

'Skyline HANDLES the approvals UI for you' (the user's explicit ask, stated as a first-class guarantee) contradicts the design's own admission that on iOS the overlay is OPTIONAL and the prompt pixels fall to the app's native UIKit chrome. The guarantee is only literally true on desktop. The design surfaces this as an open question rather than resolving it, leaving the headline promise half-met.

The foundation says the new tier 'honors batteries-with-eject because every layer is optional and additive' and 'preserves the ten-line path,' but the facets add a permanent OnOverlay seam to FrameLoop in the core Skyline.Render project — which the same design's 'whatStaysOut' forbids ('Skyline.Render must NOT gain interaction concepts'). The hook is rationalized as interaction-free, but it is still net-new permanent core API added to satisfy the optional tier, which cuts against 'the core three are untouched.'

The guide is described as 'intentionally NOT a full UI framework — the foundation underneath a modern app shell,' yet the design builds Targets, Commands, Focus, Intents, a Transfer broker, AND a composited GUI overlay with text rendering and hit-testing — which IS the substance of a UI framework. The stated scope and the delivered scope diverge.

The Transfer broker is specified as first-class (seven scopes, full policy/provenance, ITransferRepresentation.OpenReadAsync), but the design's own overallGaps confirm the byte-stream representation cannot carry a zero-copy GPU texture (project memory: textures must never round-trip to CPU), so the broker is first-class for TEXT only and needs an unplanned Skyline.Interaction.Gpu bridge to be real. A 'first-class transfer broker' that cannot move the one payload Starling actually cares about (GPU surfaces) is first-class in name only.

lens: Testability / 100%-line-coverage gate (./tools/cover.sh): can every new line be hit by either headless MSTest or the main-thread WindowedTests console harness, without forcing an [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage]?

topProblems.problem: ASYNC + IAsyncEnumerable + TaskCompletionSource handoffs have ZERO precedent in this repo and are the hardest thing to drive to 100% deterministically. I grepped src/ and tests/: there is not one 'async', 'await', 'IAsyncEnumerable', 'await foreach', or 'TaskCompletionSource' in the entire codebase today. Every line is synchronous. The design's spine is async: IInteractionShell.WatchIntentsAsync (IAsyncEnumerable), the approval await (await _ui.RequestAsync(...).ConfigureAwait(false)), and the cross-thread TaskCompletionSource<ApprovalDecision> resolve. The async state machine the compiler emits has branches that resist coverage: the ct.Register(() => Resolve(...Deny...)) cancellation path, the 'already-completed TCS' race (TrySetResult returning false), RunContinuationsAsynchronously continuation, the ExpiresAt deadline -> Deny path, and the IAsyncEnumerable enumerator-disposed-before-completion + bounded-channel drop-oldest branches. Hitting 100% of those needs fake clocks, controllable schedulers, and a way to force the lose-the-race branch — none of which exist in this repo's MSTest setup. WatchIntentsAsync's 'caller cancels mid-stream', 'channel full drops oldest', and 'producer completes while consumer is awaiting' are exactly the lines that silently sit at <100% and force an exclusion.
topProblems.fix: Mandate that EVERY async/IAsyncEnumerable line lives in Skyline.Interaction or the lightweight InProcessShell (both headless), never in windowed code, AND is made deterministic by construction: (1) inject a TimeProvider/clock so ExpiresAt and timeout paths are driven by a fake clock in MSTest, not Task.Delay; (2) build WatchIntentsAsync on System.Threading.Channels with the producer and consumer both driven synchronously in-test (write N, complete, await-foreach drains, then assert) plus explicit tests for cancel-mid-stream, drop-oldest-when-full, and dispose-before-complete; (3) for the TCS handoff, expose the resolve as an internal seam callable directly from a test thread so the 'already resolved -> TrySetResult false' and 'cancel -> Deny' branches are each hit by a direct call, not a race. Treat 'no fake-clock / no synchronous channel drain' as a design defect, because without them these lines cannot reach the gate.

topProblems.problem: The Akka actor tree (ShellActor, FocusActor, BrokerActor, SurfaceActor, source actors, supervision strategy) is a large body of coverable-only-with-Akka.TestKit code, and the repo has NO Akka and NO TestKit today. Worse, coverage-hostile lines live INSIDE actors: the SupervisorStrategy lambda's Directive.Restart branch (needs a real faulting AI actor to throw and be supervised — hard to trigger deterministically and to assert it restarted clean+ungranted), the PinnedDispatcher self-deadlock guard, the 'park the asker, un-stash on ApprovalAnswered' state, the ApprovalTimedOut/ReceiveTimeout branch, and the identity-spoof reconciliation (msg.ActorId != Sender.Path -> reject). Akka.TestKit runs on worker threads (fine for MSTest, it does not need the main thread), but message-timing-dependent lines (a Tell that races a supervision restart, a scheduled timeout) are classic coverage flakers: they pass at 100% on a fast machine and drop a line on a slow CI run, which a 100% gate turns into a red build. The design's own risk list admits 'Akka actor message plumbing is the genuine coverage hazard.'
topProblems.fix: Take the design's own escape hatch and make it load-bearing: put 100% of decision logic (FocusPolicy.BestCommandTarget, Authority.Authorizes/Ceiling/Clamp, DefaultApprovalPolicy.Evaluate, the ApprovalState machine, ApprovalGate.AuthorizeAsync, snapshot rebuild, paste gate) as pure functions / a lightweight InProcessShell in Skyline.Interaction, and drive 100% of it in headless MSTest. Then keep the Akka actors as the THINNEST possible transport — ideally each Receive<T> handler is one line that calls the already-covered pure function and Tells the result, so the actor body has almost no uncovered branches of its own. Cover the unavoidable Akka glue (supervision restart, timeout, stash/un-stash, spoof-reject) with Akka.TestKit in a separate headless test project, using TestKit's deterministic primitives (TestProbe, manual scheduler / TestScheduler.Advance for the timeout, ExpectMsg) so no test depends on wall-clock timing. If a line still can only be hit by a real race, it should not exist — refactor it to a directly-callable method. Add 'Akka' assemblies to cover.sh's include/assemblyfilter list (see below) or they will not be measured at all.

topProblems.problem: ./tools/cover.sh is HARDCODED to the three core assemblies and the design never mentions amending it. The windowed coverlet step uses --include "[Skyline]*" --include "[Skyline.Gpu]*" --include "[Skyline.Render]*" and reportgenerator uses -assemblyfilters:+Skyline;+Skyline.Gpu;+Skyline.Render. The four new assemblies (Skyline.Interaction, .Akka, .Ui, .Windowing) and their four new test projects are invisible to this script as written. Two concrete consequences: (a) the new assemblies would not be measured at all, so the '100% gate' would silently not apply to thousands of new lines — a false green; (b) the design adds Skyline.Render.FrameLoop.OnOverlay, which IS inside a measured assembly, so the new public hook property's getter/setter AND the 'OnOverlay?.Invoke(...)' call site in DriveFrame become newly-required-covered lines in Skyline.Render. The OnOverlay invoke is only exercised when a non-null callback is set, which only happens from Skyline.Interaction.Ui — meaning a Skyline.Render-only test must set OnOverlay to a stub to cover the invoke line, and a separate test must cover the null/no-op path. That is doable via CreateForTest but it is unstated work in the core assembly the design pledges to barely touch.
topProblems.fix: Make editing cover.sh part of the design: add [Skyline.Interaction]*, [Skyline.Interaction.Akka]*, [Skyline.Interaction.Ui]*, [Skyline.Interaction.Windowing]* to BOTH the windowed --include flags and the reportgenerator -assemblyfilters, register the four src + four test projects in Skyline.slnx, and split the windowed-only assemblies (.Ui, .Windowing) into the coverlet/windowed step while the headless ones (.Interaction, .Akka) go through dotnet test. For OnOverlay: add two FrameLoop.Tests cases via the existing CreateForTest seam — one asserting DriveFrame invokes a stubbed OnOverlay with the live view+encoder after the clear pass ends, one asserting the null default is a no-op — so the new core-three lines stay at 100% and the 'pure wgpu seam' claim is actually exercised.

topProblems.problem: The composited ApprovalsOverlay (DrawModal, DrawIndicator, hit-testing, glyph/quad pipeline) is real-window pixel code, and the design under-specifies how its pixels are asserted to 100%. Encode() opens a LoadOp.Load pass against a TextureView* — that part follows the proven FrameLoopTests pattern (CreateHeadless + CreateColorTarget + TextureReadback) and IS coverable headlessly. BUT the branches that need a human gesture — OnPointerDown hit-testing HitAllow/HitOnce/HitDeny against cached button rects, the 'no modal -> early return' guard, the indicator-only-no-modal branch, the Pending[^1] top-of-stack selection with multiple stacked requests, and the 'snapshot swapped mid-read' tear-free read — are stateful UI logic. Getting EACH button-hit branch, the miss-all-buttons branch, the multi-pending-stack ordering, and the auto-expire-clears-indicator branch to 100% requires either driving synthetic PointerEvents through the windowed harness (which AppWindow's RaisePointer internal seam already supports) or extracting the hit-test + state machine into a pure, headless-testable class. The design mentions TextureReadback for 'the modal pixels appear' but does not commit to covering every gesture/stack/expire branch, and those are where coverage quietly dies.
topProblems.fix: Split ApprovalsOverlay into (a) a pure ApprovalState/snapshot/hit-test/stack-ordering core in Skyline.Interaction or a no-GPU class in .Ui, covered 100% in headless MSTest by feeding synthetic pointer coordinates and asserting which request resolves with which verb — every button, every miss, every stack depth, the expire-clears-indicator path; and (b) a thin Encode() that only issues wgpu calls, covered in the WindowedTests harness with TextureReadback asserting the panel/indicator pixels land (mirroring the existing 'swapchain clear is red in readback' check). Drive the gesture resolution through AppWindow.RaisePointer (already an internal test seam in the harness) so the main-thread input path is exercised end to end. Make 'hit-testing and the consent state machine are GPU-free' an explicit rule so no gesture branch is trapped behind a real swapchain.

topProblems.problem: Skyline.Interaction.Ui and Skyline.Interaction.Windowing depend on AppWindow (a GLFW window) and Skyline.Render (a real swapchain), so AppWindowInteractionSource and the overlay's window wiring can ONLY be covered by the WindowedTests console harness — and that harness is a single linear main() program, not a test runner. Every new windowed-coverage line must be appended to tests/Skyline.WindowedTests/Program.cs as more Check(...) calls in one long script with shared mutable state and Thread.Sleep-based pacing (the existing AppHost section already needs framesB>=600 hang-guards and Cocoa-defer workarounds). Adding the interaction overlay's full surface there — subscribe to PointerInput/KeyInput/TextInput, push a pending approval, drive a pointer-down onto the Allow button, assert the TCS resolved and the modal cleared, then the indicator path, the expire path, the clipboard-mirror-on-Offer path, the paste-fallback-to-ClipboardText path — bloats a fragile single-threaded harness and risks timing flakes that a 100% gate cannot tolerate. AppWindowInteractionSource's lambda bodies (window.PointerInput += e => emit intent) are only reachable by raising real events, and the broker's 'OfferAsync also writes AppWindow.ClipboardText via AppHost.Invoke' crosses the main-thread marshal, which is exactly the kind of thread hop the harness exists to allow but which is painful to assert deterministically.
topProblems.fix: Minimize the windowed-only surface aggressively. AppWindowInteractionSource should be a 3-line adapter: AppWindow event -> call a pure mapper (PointerEvent->InteractionIntent) defined and 100%-covered in Skyline.Interaction headlessly; the windowed harness then only needs ONE Check per event kind proving the wire-up fires, not the mapping logic. The clipboard mirror should go through an injected interface (IClipboard with a SetText/GetText, defaulting to an AppWindow-backed impl) so the broker's sync-and-fallback logic is 100%-covered in headless MSTest against a fake clipboard, and the windowed harness only proves the AppWindow-backed IClipboard round-trips (which Program.cs already does: 'clipboard round-trips'). Keep the windowed harness additions to a handful of wire-up Checks with the same hang-guard discipline the existing harness uses; never put resolution/policy/mapping logic where only the harness can reach it.

topProblems.problem: The iOS approvals path (UIKitApprovalUi : IApprovalUi presenting a UIAlertController) and the iOS InputSource (UIPanGestureRecognizer/UITextField -> intents, UIPasteboard broker) are platform code that the macOS CI cover.sh cannot execute at all. The design correctly keeps the DECISION logic pixel-free and headless (good), but UIKitApprovalUi.RequestAsync's body — marshal to UIKit main thread, present alert, resolve TCS from the tap — is genuinely unrunnable in the headless/windowed vehicles on the build machine. If any of that lands in a measured assembly it forces an [ExcludeFromCodeCoverage] (the repo currently has exactly ONE such exclusion, Guard.cs, and AGENTS.md documents it as the only one). Adding a second class of exclusion ('iOS presentation') erodes the '100% with one documented exception' invariant the repo is proud of.
topProblems.fix: Keep ALL iOS-specific presentation classes (UIKitApprovalUi, the UIKit input source) out of the four core interaction assemblies entirely — put them in the iOS sample/app project (alongside StarlingMock.Ios), NOT in Skyline.Interaction.Ui, so they are never in cover.sh's scope and never need an exclusion attribute in a shipped library. The IApprovalUi seam stays in Skyline.Interaction and is 100%-covered headlessly with a fake IApprovalUi (a TCS the test resolves directly). Document explicitly that 'Skyline-shipped interaction assemblies stay 100% coverable; platform presentation lives in app/sample projects' so the one-exclusion invariant holds.

whatToKeep: The split that puts ALL decision logic (FocusPolicy.BestCommandTarget, Authority.Authorizes/Ceiling/Clamp, DefaultApprovalPolicy.Evaluate, the consent state machine, paste gate) as PURE functions in zero-dependency Skyline.Interaction is the single best coverage decision in the design. Pure functions over plain records are trivially driven to 100% in headless MSTest with no window, no GPU, no Akka — exactly the repo's strongest test vehicle. This is the right instinct and must be enforced ruthlessly: if a branch can be a pure function, it must be.

ApprovalsOverlay.Encode(TextureView* view, CommandEncoder* encoder, FrameInfo info) takes RAW pointers and a value struct, not a WindowSurface. That is the same decoupling that makes the existing FrameLoop.DriveFrame coverable: it can be driven headlessly with GpuContext.CreateHeadless + CreateColorTarget + a fabricated TextureCreateView + TextureReadback, precisely mirroring FrameLoopTests. Keep this signature shape — it is the proven seam and it lets the GPU draw path hit 100% without a real swapchain.

The immutable-snapshot-swapped-into-a-volatile-field pattern (ApprovalSnapshot mirroring AppWindow's FrameGeom) is genuinely test-friendly: the render-thread read is a single pure function of the snapshot, so 'Encode given snapshot X produces draws Y' is a deterministic, headless assertion with no thread race to cover. Keep it, and expose RebuildSnapshot as an internal seam so the snapshot-contents branches (has-modal, indicator-active, empty, multi-pending) are each covered by a direct call.

Designing the InProcessShell (lightweight non-Akka IInteractionShell) as the default and making Akka opt-in is the right move for BOTH the ten-line ethos AND coverage: it means the canonical flow can be fully exercised headlessly without pulling Akka.TestKit timing into the gate. Keep it, and make the InProcessShell the primary coverage vehicle for the shell contract so the Akka actors only need to cover their thin transport glue.

Keeping the FrameLoop.OnOverlay hook a pure wgpu seam (TextureView* + CommandEncoder*, names nothing from the interaction guide) means it is coverable through the EXISTING FrameLoop.CreateForTest seam with two small headless tests (stub-set invoke path, null no-op path) rather than needing a window. Keep the signature interaction-free so it stays inside the proven headless DriveFrame coverage pattern.
contradictions: The design says Skyline.Render's 'only sanctioned change' is one null-by-default hook that 'changes nothing for existing consumers,' yet a 100% line gate means the new OnOverlay property AND the new 'OnOverlay?.Invoke(...)' call site in DriveFrame become lines that MUST be covered in the Skyline.Render assembly. 'Changes nothing' is false for the coverage gate: it adds at least two new required-covered lines (invoke-when-set, no-op-when-null) to a core-three assembly the design pledges to barely touch. The design never accounts for covering them.

The design leans on Akka ('one guide Actor = one Akka actor with an address') as the structural enforcement of identity/focus/authority, while simultaneously admitting Akka is too heavy for the ten-line path and proposing a non-Akka InProcessShell as the default. For coverage this is contradictory: if the InProcessShell is the default and the 100%-covered vehicle, then the Akka actors' structural guarantees (single-writer FocusActor, supervision-revokes-grants, mailbox-is-identity) are NOT what the gate actually exercises — they become a second, parallel implementation whose actor-specific lines (supervision restart, stash/un-stash, dispatcher) are extra coverage burden that the pure logic does not relieve. You cannot both claim Akka provides the safety guarantees AND route coverage around Akka through a non-actor shell.

The foundation says the interaction tier must NOT leak into the core three and Skyline.Render 'gains no interaction concepts,' but the only way to cover the OnOverlay invoke line in Skyline.Render is to have a test set OnOverlay to a non-null callback that opens a LoadOp.Load pass — i.e. the core-three test must itself perform the overlay-style composite to reach 100%. The interaction tier's reason-for-existing thus reaches down into a core-three test to satisfy the gate, which is in tension with the 'second question must never leak down' rule.

The design repeatedly cites AppWindow's volatile-FrameGeom and FramePacer's zero-alloc discipline as proven patterns it mirrors, but those patterns were proven in a SYNCHRONOUS, no-async, no-Akka, no-TCS codebase. The design imports async/await, IAsyncEnumerable, TaskCompletionSource, and an actor runtime — none of which the cited proven patterns (or the existing test harnesses) have ever had to drive to 100%. Citing the synchronous patterns as evidence the async/actor design is equally coverable is an unsupported leap; the hard-to-cover surface (cancellation tokens, timeouts, channel backpressure, supervision races) is exactly the part with NO precedent in this repo.
